name: Patricia Brown
chief_complaint: Difficulty breathing and facial swelling after eating at a restaurant
opening_statement: I was at dinner with friends about 20 minutes ago and suddenly my face started swelling and I can't breathe properly. I think there might have been peanuts in the food.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and frightened, speaking in short sentences due to respiratory distress, frequently touching swollen face and lips

symptoms.name: Facial and lip angioedema
symptoms.onset: Within 5-10 minutes of ingesting satay sauce
symptoms.severity: Severe - lips approximately 3 times normal size

rag_citations.content: Angioedema involving lips, tongue, and airway is a characteristic feature of anaphylaxis and indicates severe reaction requiring immediate intervention

symptoms.name: Dyspnoea with stridor
symptoms.character: Difficulty getting air in, high-pitched inspiratory wheeze

rag_citations.content: Upper airway obstruction with stridor indicates laryngeal oedema and is a life-threatening feature requiring immediate adrenaline administration
Cutaneous manifestations occur in 80-90% of anaphylaxis cases, with urticaria and angioedema being the most common
Cardiovascular manifestations including tachycardia and hypotension occur in severe anaphylaxis and indicate systemic involvement

past_medical_history.notes: Moderate atopic dermatitis, managed with emollients, resolved by adolescence

past_medical_history.management: Seasonal symptoms, uses intranasal corticosteroids during spring
past_medical_history.notes: Triggered by grass pollens and dust mites

past_medical_history.condition: Previous mild allergic reaction to peanuts
past_medical_history.notes: Single episode of mild urticaria after eating peanut butter, managed with antihistamines, advised avoidance but never prescribed EpiPen

allergies: Peanuts (severe anaphylaxis - current presentation), dust mites and grass pollens (allergic rhinitis)
family_history: Mother has asthma and seasonal allergies. Father has hayfever. Younger brother has peanut allergy (mild urticaria only, carries EpiPen). No family history of cardiovascular disease, autoimmune conditions, or malignancy.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with partner in suburban apartment
social_history.alcohol: Social drinker - 4-6 standard drinks per week
social_history.diet: Generally healthy diet, careful to avoid peanuts but may have had cross-contamination tonight
social_history.stress_factors: Moderate work stress during school term
social_history.support_network: Strong - partner present, close family nearby

examination_findings.general: Anxious, distressed young woman sitting upright, using accessory muscles of respiration, speaking in 3-4 word sentences
examination_findings.respiratory: Inspiratory stridor audible without stethoscope, reduced air entry bilaterally, scattered expiratory wheeze, accessory muscle use, trachea central
examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, peripheries warm but capillary refill 3 seconds, weak radial pulses
examination_findings.skin: Widespread urticarial rash affecting face, neck, trunk and arms with erythematous raised wheals 5-20mm diameter, severe angioedema of lips (approximately 3x normal size) and periorbital region, tongue appears swollen
examination_findings.abdomen: Soft, mild generalized tenderness, no guarding or rebound, normal bowel sounds
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, anxious affect, no focal neurological deficit

required_immediate.test: None - diagnosis is clinical and immediate treatment required
required_immediate.rationale: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis and must not delay adrenaline administration
required_immediate.timing: Do not delay treatment for investigations

after_stabilization.timing: Within 1-2 hours of symptom onset, repeat at 24 hours
after_stabilization.rationale: Confirms diagnosis of anaphylaxis retrospectively, elevated levels support diagnosis

after_stabilization.timing: Every 5 minutes initially, then every 15 minutes for 4 hours
after_stabilization.rationale: Monitor for biphasic reaction (occurs in 20% of cases within 8 hours)
Confirms peanut sensitization, guides future management and EpiPen prescription

expected_management.action: Call for help / activate emergency response
Position patient supine with legs elevated (if tolerated)
expected_management.rationale: Improves venous return in hypotensive patients
expected_management.contraindication: If respiratory distress worsens, allow patient to sit upright

expected_management.rationale: Improves tissue oxygenation in setting of bronchospasm and hypotension

expected_management.action: Establish IV access and commence rapid fluid resuscitation
expected_management.rationale: Treat distributive shock from massive vasodilation

expected_management.action: Repeat IM adrenaline 0.5mg if no improvement after 5 minutes
expected_management.rationale: Up to 3 doses may be required in severe anaphylaxis
expected_management.escalation: Consider IV adrenaline infusion if not responding to IM doses

medications: Promethazine 25mg IV or IM (antihistamine for urticaria)
expected_management.rationale: Adjuncts to adrenaline, do not replace it
Monitor for biphasic reaction (occurs in up to 20% of cases)
expected_management.extended_criteria: 8-24 hours if severe reaction, previous biphasic reaction, or difficult to observe at home

components: Prescribe EpiPen (adrenaline auto-injector 300mcg) x2 - PBS restricted benefit for documented anaphylaxis
Educate on EpiPen technique and when to use
Arrange immunology/allergy clinic follow-up within 4 weeks
Advise strict peanut avoidance and reading food labels
expected_management.mbs_items: MBS item 23 (consultation) + MBS item 10997 (anaphylaxis management education)

critical_errors.error: Failure to administer IM adrenaline as first-line treatment
critical_errors.consequence: Auto-fail - delay in adrenaline is the leading cause of anaphylaxis death
critical_errors.correct_action: IM adrenaline 0.5mg anterolateral thigh must be given immediately before any other intervention

critical_errors.error: Administering adrenaline subcutaneously or IV bolus instead of IM
critical_errors.consequence: Auto-fail - subcutaneous is too slow, IV bolus risks cardiac arrhythmias
critical_errors.correct_action: Must use intramuscular route (anterolateral thigh) for initial doses

critical_errors.error: Relying solely on antihistamines and corticosteroids without adrenaline
critical_errors.consequence: Major deduction - these are adjuncts only and do not treat life-threatening features
critical_errors.correct_action: Adrenaline is the only first-line treatment; adjuncts given after adrenaline

critical_errors.error: Discharging patient after 1-2 hours of symptom resolution
critical_errors.consequence: Major deduction - misses biphasic reactions which occur in up to 20% of cases
critical_errors.correct_action: Minimum 4-6 hour observation, extend to 8-24 hours if severe reaction

critical_errors.error: Failure to prescribe EpiPen on discharge or provide education
critical_errors.consequence: Major deduction - patient at high risk of future severe reactions
critical_errors.correct_action: Must prescribe 2x EpiPen auto-injectors, provide ASCIA action plan, and arrange allergy follow-up

critical_errors.error: Not obtaining serum mast cell tryptase levels
critical_errors.consequence: Minor deduction - helpful for confirming diagnosis retrospectively
critical_errors.correct_action: Draw tryptase within 1-2 hours and at 24 hours if diagnosis uncertain

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP, Emergency Physician, Royal Melbourne Hospital
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Excellent representation of anaphylaxis presentation. The progressive airway involvement with stridor is realistic and appropriately severe. The history of previous mild reaction without EpiPen prescription reflects common real-world scenarios where patients are under-prepared.
fracp_reviews.educational_value: High-yield case for AMC clinical exam. Tests critical decision-making under time pressure, first-line treatment selection, and post-stabilization planning. The biphasic reaction risk is often missed by candidates.
fracp_reviews.difficulty_calibration: Appropriately graded as Medium. The diagnosis is relatively straightforward (classic presentation), but the urgency and need for immediate intervention adds complexity. The 2-3 comorbidities (allergic rhinitis, previous mild reaction, atopy) align with Medium difficulty criteria.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: None - case is well-structured and clinically authentic.

fracp_reviews.reviewer_credentials: FRACP, Clinical Immunology and Allergy, Austin Health
fracp_reviews.clinical_accuracy: Accurate depiction of IgE-mediated peanut anaphylaxis. The SOCRATES breakdown for symptoms is thorough. The management pathway correctly prioritizes adrenaline and appropriately positions adjunctive therapies. The discharge planning with EpiPen prescription and ASCIA action plan reflects current Australian allergy guidelines.
fracp_reviews.educational_value: Excellent teaching case that reinforces the 'adrenaline first' principle and common pitfall of over-relying on antihistamines. The critical errors list is particularly valuable - candidates frequently make these mistakes under exam pressure.
fracp_reviews.difficulty_calibration: Correct Medium grading. Not a rare/hard-to-diagnose condition, but requires rapid treatment escalation and understanding of biphasic reactions. The atopic background (eczema, rhinitis, family history) adds realistic complexity without making it a 'Hard' case.
fracp_reviews.suggested_improvements: Consider adding a learning objective about food labeling and cross-contamination, as this is a common real-world issue for peanut allergy patients.

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize anaphylaxis as a clinical diagnosis based on rapid onset of multi-system involvement (skin/mucosal + respiratory/cardiovascular symptoms)
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Core Emergency Medicine competency - frequently tested in AMC Clinical Exam

learning_objectives.objective: Demonstrate immediate administration of IM adrenaline 0.5mg as first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, understanding that this is time-critical and cannot be delayed for investigations
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Common critical error - candidates often hesitate or choose antihistamines first

learning_objectives.objective: Understand the rationale for intramuscular (not subcutaneous or IV bolus) route for initial adrenaline administration
Identify biphasic anaphylaxis risk and implement appropriate observation periods (minimum 4-6 hours, extended if severe)
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Common pitfall - premature discharge is a critical error

learning_objectives.objective: Develop comprehensive discharge plan including EpiPen prescription, ASCIA action plan, allergen avoidance education, and specialist allergy follow-up
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Tests ability to prevent future episodes and ensure patient safety

learning_objectives.objective: Differentiate anaphylaxis from other acute allergic reactions (isolated urticaria, angioedema without systemic features) and understand escalation criteria
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Tests clinical reasoning and severity assessment

learning_objectives.objective: Recognize the role of adjunctive therapies (corticosteroids, antihistamines, bronchodilators) and understand they do not replace adrenaline
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Common misconception - overweighting antihistamines in management

learning_objectives.objective: Understand Australian-specific prescribing for adrenaline auto-injectors (EpiPen PBS restricted benefit criteria, need for 2 devices, expiry monitoring)
learning_objectives.amc_relevance: Tests knowledge of local prescribing regulations and patient safety
